back: A large, steep-sided dome of massive granite or gneiss rising abruptly from a plain; an inselberg.
Kopje: small hill of piled rounded blocks. Tor: free-standing stack of rounded blocks on a hilltop or slope. Both are smaller than bornhardts.
Stage 1: deep chemical weathering along joints beneath the surface. Stage 2: stripping of the regolith exposes the unweathered massive cores as domes.
Scarp retreat (King's pediplanation) leaves residual hills on a pediplain; pressure release forms sheeting joints (exfoliation) on domes.
Close joints let water in and cause deep weathering; wide joints or massive rock resist and survive as hills. It is the control common to all theories.
A hard crust formed by concentration of minerals in soil; laterite is iron and aluminium oxides left after leaching of silica, hardened by wet-dry cycles.
Landscape formed by solution of soluble rock (limestone) with caves, sinkholes, underground drainage and distinctive hills.
Cockpit karst: star-shaped depressions among hills. Cone karst: many conical hills. Tower karst: isolated steep towers on a flat plain.
Heavy rainfall and soil carbon dioxide from dense vegetation make strong carbonic acid, so solution along joints is rapid.
